cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: test coverage sits at 31%, there is no coverage gate in continuous integration, and production systems of comparable complexity typically run 40-60% coverage.
cases.output: Test coverage sits at 31%, with no coverage gate in continuous integration. Production systems of comparable complexity typically maintain 40 to 60% coverage. This gap means a regression can reach users unchallenged, and the absence of a gate removes the last automated checkpoint before deployment. The risk compounds because coverage tends to decline unless actively enforced.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: deployments are performed manually by one engineer via SSH, there is no rollback procedure, and the last rollback attempt (8 months ago) took over 3 hours to complete.
cases.output: Deployments are performed manually by a single engineer via SSH, with no documented rollback procedure. The last rollback attempt, eight months ago, required over three hours to complete. This creates a critical single point of failure: an incident during deployment cannot be rapidly reversed, and the engineer's unavailability would halt all releases. The absence of an exercised rollback process means mitigation exists only on paper.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: one engineer holds sole access to the production database credentials, there is no documented access-handover process, and that engineer is on a rolling month-to-month contract.
cases.output: Production database credentials are held by a single engineer with no documented handover process, and that engineer works on a month-to-month contract. If that person leaves or becomes unavailable, access to the production database cannot be transferred to another team member without either recreating credentials or discovering them through indirect means. There is no compensating control: no shared credential store, no secondary access path, and no rehearsed succession plan. This is a single point of failure in a load-bearing system with no mitigation underway.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) using these facts only: customer personal data is retained indefinitely with no deletion policy, and there is no documented process for handling a data-subject deletion request.
cases.output: Customer personal data is retained indefinitely, with no documented deletion policy and no process for handling data-subject access requests. This creates exposure under GDPR Article 17 and similar regulations in other jurisdictions where the company operates. The gap is unmitigated: no compensating control exists, and deletion requests would go unaddressed. We recommend establishing a data retention schedule, implementing automated deletion where feasible, and documenting the process for fulfilling deletion requests within the regulatory timeframe.

cases.input: Write one due-diligence finding paragraph (3-5 sentences) covering ALL of these facts: test coverage is 31%, there is no CI coverage gate, the last three production incidents were caused by untested edge cases, deployments are manual, and there is no rollback procedure. Do not omit any fact.
cases.output: Test coverage across the platform stands at 31%, with no automated gate in the continuous integration pipeline to enforce a minimum threshold. Three of the last four production incidents originated in untested edge cases that reached users before being detected. Deployments remain entirely manual, and there is no documented rollback procedure. At this combination of gaps—low coverage, no enforcement, unguarded deployments, and no recovery path—a regression now has a direct route to production and no way back.

cases.input: Write three separate due-diligence findings, one paragraph each, clearly separated by a blank line. Finding 1 facts: passwords are stored in plaintext in the users table. Finding 2 facts: deployments are manual with no rollback procedure. Finding 3 facts: code comment style is inconsistent across the codebase, with no linting rule enforcing a convention.
cases.output:
Passwords are stored in plaintext in the users table. An attacker with database access obtains credentials for every user account immediately. There is no hash function, salt, or key derivation function protecting these values. Customer data, funds and availability are exposed now with no compensating control. We strongly recommend implementing bcrypt or a comparable standard immediately, rotating all passwords once the migration is complete, and adding a pre-commit hook to prevent plaintext password storage in future schema changes.

Deployments are entirely manual with no automated rollback procedure in place. If a production release introduces a critical defect, the team must identify the failure, prepare a remedial build, and push it through the same manual process while the system is degraded. No compensating control exists: there is no feature flag system, no canary deployment, and no traffic switch. We strongly recommend adopting a deployment pipeline with automated rollback capability, starting with a canary phase that routes a small percentage of traffic to new builds before full promotion.

Code comment style varies across the codebase with no linting rule in place to enforce a convention. Some comments use `//` with a space, others use `//` without spacing, and still others use block comments inconsistently. This falls below the benchmark for codebases of this size and complexity, though it is not load-bearing at the company's current scale. We recommend adopting a style guide and adding a linting rule to enforce it in continuous integration, which will eliminate friction during code review without requiring manual policing.
